messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Elias Vance was thirty-two when the desert convoy turned into an ambush during his second tour as a relief worker in a fractured republic. What began as a routine aid drop dissolved into chaotic crossfire in a narrow market alley, the kind of space where every turn suddenly became a choke point. He remembered the sudden snap of gunfire, the dust coating his throat, and the terrifying realization that the people moving toward him could be civilians or combatants until it was too late. When he finally slipped through a cracked rear gate and collapsed in an adjacent courtyard, he learned a stark lesson: survival depended on knowing every possible egress before stepping into a new space, and the casual proximity of others could instantly shift from neutral to lethal. Two years later, now working as a firefighter in a suburban station, Elias found his nervous system still operating on that old frequency. He could not explain why his pulse would spike the moment a caller’s husband approached the fire truck to relay the address, nor why stepping into his own living room felt like entering a trap. He had come to believe that danger did not retire with the sun. At the station, he mapped every fire escape and side door the second his boots hit the threshold, his eyes darting to the apparatus bay’s roll-up door and the stairwell behind the locker room. At home, he sat on the edge of the couch, his back to the wall, scanning the front door and the basement stairs as if they might suddenly yield him a way out. The fear of strangers had hardened into a reflex; even a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder made his shoulders lock, his mind instantly scripting worst-case scenarios. To keep the panic at bay, Elias built a careful architecture of avoidance. He stopped taking the running routes he used to log before his deployment, telling himself the apartment complex stairs were too confining, though the real reason was that elevated heart rates felt like the opening warning of a firefight. He refused to let himself enjoy the quiet Sunday mornings his wife cooked for him, pushing away any warmth because peace felt like a trap waiting to spring. Most of all, he kept himself perpetually poised by the nearest door in every room he entered. His careful avoidance had quietly rewritten his nervous system’s rules. Every time he stayed near a door instead of letting himself relax, every time he refused to run or pushed away the quiet comfort his wife offered, he starved his mind of the evidence that he was safe. Those safety behaviors did not quiet his fears; they directly fed them, sharpening his threat detection until every shadow felt like the open alley again. The loop tightened without him noticing. When a structure fire broke out three blocks from the station, the roar of the engines usually grounded him, but this time, scanning the streets for alternative evacuations consumed half his attention. He delayed relaying critical information to dispatch because he was too busy assessing the structural exits of the adjacent shopping center, a hesitation that cost him a colleague’s sharp look and left his wife wondering why he no longer seemed present even in their own kitchen. What frightened him most was not the fire itself, but the creeping certainty that his own precautions were the only things keeping him from being overwhelmed. Every time he checked the perimeter instead of letting his shoulders drop, he deepened the fear that he could never truly rest. By the time Elias scheduled his first appointment, the quiet at home had become unbearable. He had come to believe that if he stopped checking the exits, the past would finally catch up to him, and he was terrified that his marriage was fraying faster than his own nerves. He did not want to be labeled broken; he wanted to know how to stop waiting for the next explosion, and to find a way to sit on his own couch without his hands trembling.
